metaDescription: Six cordless hedge trimmers from Milwaukee, Makita, Skil, Worx, Greenworks and Black+Decker, compared on blade, cut capacity and battery platform.
expertTake: The Milwaukee M18 FUEL is the best choice for anyone already on that battery, and the Skil PWR CORE 40 kit is the best complete package for a newcomer. The Worx 22 inch is the value pick for small yards. If your hedges are thick and woody, skip the whole category and buy loppers first.
introParagraphs: A cordless hedge trimmer is a simple tool with one hidden decision: the battery family you are buying into. The blade, the gap between its teeth and the tip weight matter, but the platform decides whether the tool is cheap or costly over five years.

Most buyers overshoot on blade length and undershoot on capacity. A long blade covers more ground per pass, but it does not cut thicker stems. This guide ranks six machines by what they cut, how they handle and what they commit you to.

products.name: Milwaukee 2726-20 M18 FUEL Cordless Hedge Trimmer, Bare Tool
products.description:
Milwaukee's trimmer is a bare tool aimed at people who already own M18 batteries. The brushless FUEL motor runs cooler under load than a brushed design and holds speed as the blade meets thicker stems, and the 3/4 inch capacity is the figure to compare against the rest of this lineup.

What it is not is a starter kit. The listing says battery and charger are not included, so a first-time buyer pays for both, and by that point the 40V kits below look like better value. It earns its place for the buyer with five or six M18 tools in the shed, where one battery pool serves the drill, blower and trimmer.

Over three years the parts that fail are rarely the motor. Resin on the blades and a bent bar are the usual causes of stalling, so wipe the blades after each use and store the pack indoors. The 18V M18 pack is also a convenient size, small enough that the trimmer does not feel rear-heavy the way some 40V packs do. Compared with the Makita at 24 inches, this is the safer pick if you prefer one battery for everything, though the Makita trims a wider swath per pass.
products.bestFor: Existing M18 owners who want one more tool for the same packs.
pros: Brushless motor holds speed in thick growth
Runs on the common M18 battery family
3/4 in. cut capacity on a handheld body
Bare tool avoids paying for a duplicate pack
cons: Battery and charger are sold separately
Blade length is shorter than the 40V options

products.name: Makita 40V Max XGT 24 in. Brushless Hedge Trimmer, Bare Tool

specList.label: Claimed runtime
specList.value: Up to 6 h on a 4.0Ah pack

products.description:
The standout feature here is the three-speed switch. Low is 2,000 strokes per minute, medium 3,600 and high 5,000, so you can drop to the low setting on delicate topiary or soft growth and save charge, then use full speed on a dense flat top. No other trimmer in this lineup lets you trade pace for runtime so directly.

The cost is the platform. It is a bare tool on Makita's 40V XGT family, which is separate from Makita's 18V LXT line, so owners of the smaller packs cannot use their batteries. The claim of up to 6 hours is with a 4.0Ah pack under light load and should be taken as a ceiling. At 24 inches the head is also long for overhead work.

Ownership follows the usual pattern for a brushless tool: very little motor attention, but consistent blade care. Oil the cutting edges and do not leave the pack on a charger for weeks. The speed dial is the thing to check on a used tool, since a dial that sticks between settings affects control. If you cut mostly soft, fast-growing privet, expect to live on the middle 3,600 setting, which gives most of the speed at lower battery draw than the top setting.
products.bestFor: Owners who value adjustable speed and already use Makita XGT packs.
pros: Three speed settings from 2,000 to 5,000 SPM
24 inch blade for fast passes on flat tops
Brushless motor with strong claimed runtime
Speed control extends battery life on easy cuts
cons: XGT packs are separate from 18V Makita tools
Bare tool with no battery or charger

products.name: Skil PWR CORE 40 Brushless 24 in. Hedge Trimmer Kit with 2.5Ah Battery
products.description:
Skil sells this as a complete kit, which sets it apart from the two bare-tool premium models. A 2.5Ah 40V battery and the Auto PWR JUMP charger come in the box, and a 24 inch dual-action blade with a 3/4 inch cut puts it in the same class as the Makita at a more approachable total cost.

The PWR CORE 40 pack wraps each cell with cooling, which is a sensible design for a tool that runs flat out through long hedge lines, because heat is what shortens lithium life. A 2.5Ah pack is modest, though: for a long boundary you will want a spare. Next to the Worx at 22 inches, the Skil adds blade length and capacity but weighs more in the hand.

Since the platform is newer than the older Greenworks or Black+Decker ranges, check that a spare pack and a replacement blade are easy to source before committing. Clean the blade after use and keep the pack out of freezing sheds.
products.bestFor: A first-time buyer who wants a complete 24 inch brushless kit.
pros: Battery and charger included in the box
Brushless digital motor runs cool
24 inch dual-action blade with 3/4 in. cut
Cell cooling on the PWR CORE 40 pack
cons: 2.5Ah pack is small for long hedges
Platform is less widely stocked than older ones

products.name: Worx WG261 20V 22 in. Cordless Hedge Trimmer, 5.5 lb
products.description:
The Worx WG261 is the light one. At 5.5 pounds with a 22 inch dual-action blade it is easier to hold at chest height than any 24 inch trimmer here, and a shorter reach keeps the tip from swinging on corners. For a small to medium garden that is a better trade than extra blade length.

It rides on Worx's Power Share battery, which the maker says powers 75 plus tools across 20V, 40V and 80V. The listing includes a 2.0Ah pack, which is modest, so a long hedge may need the pack swapped midway. Against the Black+Decker 22 inch with its 3/4 inch capacity, the Worx is aimed at the same garden but weighs less than the heavier 40V kits.

The usual caution applies: thick woody stems will stall any 20V machine, so keep it for green growth. Rinse resin off the blade after each use, since resin is what makes small trimmers feel underpowered. Because the pack is shared with mowers and blowers in the same range, a household can run a single charger shelf instead of one per tool, which is a quiet saving that reviews rarely mention. Buy a second pack early if the hedge is longer than about fifteen metres, since swapping beats waiting two hours for a recharge.
products.bestFor: Small to mid-sized gardens where weight matters more than reach.
pros: 5.5 lb body is easy on the arms
22 inch blade covers tops quickly
Battery shared across a large tool range
Dual-action cut keeps vibration lower
cons: 2.0Ah pack ends a long hedge early

products.name: Greenworks 40V 24 in. Cordless Hedge Trimmer, 1 in. Cut, Tool Only
products.description:
A 1 inch cutting capacity is the headline, and it is the largest figure in this lineup. The extra 1/4 inch over the Milwaukee or Skil is real money for anyone with older privet or laurel hedges that have thickened over the years, and a three-sided wraparound handle gives more places to grip when the blade is angled.

But it is sold tool only, so you need a Greenworks 40V battery and charger. Those packs are used across a wide range of the brand's mowers, blowers and trimmers, so a household with other Greenworks tools may already own them. If you do not, pricing it as a kit puts it close to the Skil.

At 24 inches the head is long, so overhead work wears the shoulders. Check the blade for loose bolts each season, and wipe the teeth after cutting resinous hedges, since sticky teeth reduce the capacity that is the reason to buy this model.
products.bestFor: Overgrown hedges with stems close to an inch thick.
pros: 1 in. capacity is the largest in the lineup
Three-sided handle gives flexible grip angles
24 inch blade for wide passes
Fits the wider 40V tool family
cons: Long blade is tiring above shoulder height

buyingCriteria.explanation: Capacity is the stem diameter the tooth gap will take, and it is the first thing to check. The Greenworks lists 1 inch while the Milwaukee and Skil list 3/4 inch. Blade length only widens the pass, so a 24 inch blade with 3/4 inch capacity will not clear a thick stem a 1 inch gap can.

A bare tool is only cheap if you own the packs. The Milwaukee M18, Makita XGT and Greenworks 40V are all bare-tool listings here, while the Skil and Worx include a pack. Compare the full cost of tool, battery and charger before deciding, and never assume two 40V families are compatible.

Weight matters over a 20 minute session more than the number on the box suggests. The Worx is listed at 5.5 pounds with a 22 inch blade, while 24 inch trimmers push more mass out in front. Long blades suit waist-height runs, and shorter ones suit corners and overhead work.

A brushless motor wastes less energy as heat and has no brushes to wear, so it holds speed better in dense growth. The Milwaukee, Makita and Skil are brushless. Brushed motors suit small yards, but if your hedge is long and you use it often, brushless pays back in cooler running and longer pack life.

A trimmer that cannot slow down wastes charge on easy cuts. The Makita offers 2,000, 3,600 and 5,000 strokes per minute, so you can save battery on soft growth. Brand runtime claims such as up to 6 hours assume a 4.0Ah pack and light work, so treat them as a ceiling.

A wraparound handle lets you rotate the blade to cut vertical sides without twisting your wrist. The Greenworks uses a three-sided grip. Look for a rear handle that can rotate or a front grip that lets you work with the blade vertical, because comfort at an odd angle decides how long you can keep going.

specDecoder.meaning: Strokes per minute is how many times the blades travel in a minute with no load. Higher is a smoother cut on soft growth, but torque under load matters more in dense stems.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Makita lists 5,000 SPM at its top setting and 2,000 at the lowest.

specDecoder.meaning: The widest stem the teeth will take. It is set by tooth gap, not motor power.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Greenworks is listed at 1 inch and the Milwaukee and Skil at 3/4 inch.

specDecoder.meaning: Amp-hours measure battery capacity. Multiply by voltage for energy, so a 2.5Ah 40V pack holds about 100 watt-hours nominal.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Skil kit ships with a 2.5Ah pack and the Worx with 2.0Ah.

specDecoder.meaning: The motor uses electronic commutation instead of carbon brushes. It runs cooler and wears less.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Milwaukee 2726-20, Makita and Skil are listed as brushless.

specDecoder.meaning: The listing includes only the machine. You must supply a compatible battery and charger.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Milwaukee, Makita and Greenworks here are all sold that way.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity and cutting speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared listed cut capacity and stroke rate. The Greenworks stood out at 1 inch while the Makita offered the fastest top speed at 5,000 SPM. Capacity counted more than speed.

howWeEvaluated.title: Total cost to use
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at whether a battery and charger came in the box. The Skil and Worx are kits, while three others are bare tools. A tool with no battery loses points for first-time buyers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered blade length against stated weight where available. The Worx at 5.5 pounds scored high for lightness. Handle shape and the ability to rotate to vertical cuts also mattered.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform strength
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered how widely each battery family is used for other tools. The Milwaukee M18 and the Worx Power Share range scored well for the breadth of tools they run. Narrower platforms lost points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership over three years
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered motor type, blade care and battery storage based on owner feedback patterns. Brushless motors scored higher for durability. Resin care is the same on every model.

Kit with battery at a low tier

cards.label: Kit
cards.text: The Skil and Worx include a battery and charger. You can start cutting the day it arrives, but you are locked into whatever pack is supplied.

cards.label: Bare tool
cards.text: The Milwaukee, Makita and Greenworks assume you own packs. They save money for existing owners and cost more for newcomers.

howToChoose.note: Newcomers pick a kit; owners of M18, XGT or Greenworks 40V pick the matching bare tool.

rows: Long runs, want to save charge

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for the widest cut capacity and a motor that holds speed under load, because stalling is the main failure with woody stems. A brushless motor and a sharp, clean blade help most.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Greenworks 40V 24 in. gives the widest capacity at 1 inch, and the Milwaukee 2726-20 offers brushless torque at 3/4 inch. Anything thicker than 1 inch still needs a lopper.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you hedge weekly and need runtime and cooler running, which suggests the Makita XGT or Milwaukee FUEL with a good battery.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if your hedge is small and tidy. The Worx WG261 does the job at 5.5 lb and the extra capacity of the others goes unused.

maintenance.why: Sap hardens on the teeth and reduces capacity. A light oil coat also protects the steel from rust.
Loose bolts let the blades gap and tear stems instead of cutting. Retighten to the maker's setting.
Cold reduces capacity and a full charge in storage ages the cells. Keep it at partial charge and dry.

maintenance.task: Clear vents and the motor housing
maintenance.why: Clippings pack into vents and trap heat. Brush them out with the battery removed.
A bent bar causes stalling that looks like a weak motor. Straighten or replace it.

faq.q: How do I choose between a kit and a bare tool?
faq.a: If you own no batteries from the brand, buy a kit such as the Skil or Worx. If you already own M18, XGT or Greenworks 40V packs, the bare tool saves you from paying twice.

faq.q: What is a fair budget for a good cordless trimmer?
faq.a: Expect to pay more for a brushless 24 inch tool than a 20V 22 inch one. The Worx is the cheapest here and the bare Milwaukee and Makita are the dearest, with kits in between.

faq.q: How long will the pack and blades last?
faq.a: With care a pack gives several seasons, and blades last years if kept clean. Avoid storing at full charge and clean sap from the teeth each time.

faq.q: Does a longer blade cut thicker branches?
faq.a: No. Capacity depends on tooth gap, so a 24 inch blade with 3/4 inch capacity is no better on thick stems than a shorter blade with the same gap.
Not by name alone. Higher voltage platforms usually store more energy and run longer, but cutting force depends on motor and gearing, so compare capacity and motor type instead.
Only soft stems up to the listed capacity, which is 3/4 inch to 1 inch here. Heavier limbs need loppers or a pole saw.
